Issued at 505 AM CDT Sat Sep 5 2026

A mid to upper level ridge axis resides over the Red River 
Valley early this morning, with a lee surface trough/low 
analyzed over far eastern Montana. A strong low level jet 
underneath the mid/upper ridge supplying warm air advection and
moisture transport has produced a corridor of isolated to 
scattered thunderstorms from northwest North Dakota through the 
James River Valley. Storms in the northwest have been strong to 
severe at times and are producing torrential rainfall. This 
activity is likely to persist and continue drifting eastward 
through the morning as low level flow remains southerly. 

The lee trough/low is forecast to slide into the western 
Dakotas today, accompanied by the thermal ridge. Highs in the 
90s are forecast along and to the south and west of the 
Missouri River, hottest in the southwest where lower dewpoints 
are forecast. Areas along and to the north and east of the 
river are likely to see daytime dewpoints in the mid 60s to 
lower 70s, which could push maximum heat indices near 100 along
the Missouri River Valley, south of Lake Sakakawea. 
Deterministic guidance notes persistent low level warm air 
advection in the eastern half of the state throughout the day 
today, with subtle shortwave impulses climbing the top of the 
ridge. Because of this forcing, daytime convection aside from 
what is ongoing this morning cannot be ruled out. But rising 
mid level height tendencies along with very strong MLCIN seem 
likely to suppress convective initiation through the afternoon, 
which is the outcome that has the greatest support from CAMs. 
If a surface or mixed-layer based storm were to develop, it 
could have access to at least 3000 J/kg CAPE and deep layer 
shear around 30-40 kts. This leaves a conditional risk for 
isolated severe thunderstorms in the forecast for today. For 
this evening into tonight, the low level jet could once again 
initiate elevated convection. This seems most likely to occur 
over the southern half of the state where warm air advection is
strongest, but the RAP also shows a strong plume of poleward 
theta-e advection across the north. Most CAMs predict that any 
nocturnal elevated convection is unlikely to tap into the 
maximum potential buoyancy and shear, but the 06Z HRRR is a 
noted outlier in bringing a cluster of strong to severe storms 
through south central and southeast North Dakota this evening. 

The lee surface low is forecast to sag southward and settle 
over the Black Hills on Sunday, maintaining a broad southeast 
to easterly surface flow reinforcing the moisture-rich air mass.
The NBM keeps highs in the 80s to lower 90s, but this seems a 
little too warm conceptually. It will nevertheless be another 
unseasonably warm and very humid day, with dewpoints remaining 
in the mid 60s to lower 70s. The convective forecast during the 
day Sunday is similar to that of today, with two exceptions 
being 1) falling rather than rising mid level height tendencies 
and 2) stronger deep layer shear. But the lack of a strong 
forcing mechanism combined with strong CIN keeps thunderstorm 
probabilities low until later in the day Sunday, although the 
NBM does maintain a broad expanse of 30 to 40 percent PoPs 
across all but southwest North Dakota. Heading into Sunday 
night, shortwave energy ejecting from the base of a deep 
western CONUS longwave trough will reach the Northern High 
Plains, resulting in increased probabilities for showers and 
thunderstorms. CAMs that reach this forecast time range do 
support a risk for strong to severe thunderstorms, favoring 
western North Dakota during the evening hours. These storms 
would likely be rooted at the base of an elevated mixed layer 
with strong MUCAPE and effective bulk shear. 

On Monday, a closed upper low sitting at the base of the 
western CONUS trough is forecast to lift northeastward and 
interact with a shortwave ejecting northeast off the Northern 
Rockies and a separate upper low over southern British Columbia.
Broad lee cyclogenesis combined with strong low level warm air 
advection and mid level height falls will bring much higher 
chances for showers and thunderstorms across the state late 
Sunday night through Labor Day. Ensemble guidance still favors 
the northern half of the state for higher rainfall amounts as 
southwest and south central North Dakota remain favored to be 
dry slotted. However, prior to the arrival of the dry slot, 
deterministic guidance is beginning to hone in on a strong cold 
frontal passage that could potentially support an all hazards 
severe event if requisite ingredients can become spatially and 
temporally aligned. 

The strongest vort max is forecast to swing from Montana to 
Manitoba Monday night into Tuesday, but the dry slot from the 
preceding cyclone could keep all but far northern parts of our 
forecast area rain free over this time period. Cooler high
